claim: NCERT Class XI Indian Economic Development names MSP as one of three policy instruments, listed as the fourth element of agricultural marketing, with buffer stocks of wheat and rice kept by the Food Corporation of India and distribution of foodgrains and sugar through the PDS
value: Instruments listed: (i) assurance of minimum support prices (MSP) for agricultural products (ii) buffer stocks of wheat and rice by FCI (iii) PDS distribution. Aim stated: protect farmers' income and give foodgrains to the poor at a subsidised rate
as_of: NCERT keec1 Revised Edition Jan 2023, Reprint Feb 2026 (2026-27)
source: NCERT, Indian Economic Development (Class XI), ch.5 Rural Development, sec 5.4 Agricultural Market System
note: Read in full. This is the main NCERT passage. It gives no definition of MSP, no crop list, no cost formula, no procurement numbers. NCERT: 'The fourth element is the policy instruments like (i) ... (ii) ... (iii) ...'. Audit fix 2 Nov 2026.

claim: The same NCERT chapter says that despite government intervention private trade (moneylenders, rural political elites, big merchants, rich farmers) predominates agricultural markets
value: Statement made in NCERT's own words; no figure or year given
as_of: NCERT keec1 Reprint 2026-27 (text unchanged from 2023 revision)
note: NCERT claim, undated. Do not present as current. Compare CACP data on share of output bought at MSP (claims P12-P17).

claim: NCERT notes that in 2020 Parliament passed three laws to reform agricultural marketing, that some farmers supported and the rest opposed them, and that the Acts were later repealed; it asks students to collect details and debate
value: Three laws passed 2020; later repealed; discussion prompt only; the three laws are not named
source: NCERT keec105 'Work This Out' box after sec 5.4
second_source: Farm Laws Repeal Bill 2021 (Bill No.143 of 2021) Statement of Objects
note: The Bill names the three Acts (see L10). NCERT leaves the debate to the teacher.

claim: NCERT Class XI ch.2 (Indian Economy 1950-1990) says the Green Revolution produced a marketed surplus of rice and wheat that sold in the market, food-grain prices fell relative to other items, and the government could procure enough grain to build a stock for shortages
value: Concepts: marketed surplus (portion of produce sold by farmers); falling relative price of foodgrains; procurement to build stock
source: NCERT keec102 ch.2 Indian Economy 1950-1990, section 'The Green Revolution'
note: The only place NCERT links procurement to the Green Revolution. Origin story for why MSP and procurement started (see L01 and the HLC 2015 summary for the 1965 origin of the Agricultural Prices Commission and FCI).

claim: NCERT Class X Geography (Contemporary India II) ch.4 Agriculture has exactly one sentence on MSP: the government announces minimum support price, remunerative and procurement prices for important crops to check exploitation of farmers by speculators and middlemen
value: One sentence, under institutional reforms; no definitions, no numbers
as_of: NCERT jess1 Revised Edition Nov 2022, Reprint Dec 2025 (2026-27)
source: NCERT jess104 ch.4 Agriculture, section on technological and institutional reforms
page_or_section: chapter PDF p.10 of 13 (printed page number not captured in text layer)
note: 'Remunerative' and 'procurement' prices are old (pre-MSP-era) terms. Present MSP policy no longer uses them as separate prices; do not teach them as current categories without a source.

claim: NCERT Class X Understanding Economic Development ch.1 mentions 'higher support prices' only as a stated developmental goal of prosperous farmers in a table of different people's goals
value: One phrase; no explanation of MSP
source: NCERT jess201 ch.1 Development, table of developmental goals
note: Useful only as the 'different people want different things' hook: a farmer's goal (higher price) is a consumer's cost.

claim: NCERT Class XI ch.3 (Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal) lists 'low minimum support price' among policy changes that, with lower import duties on farm goods, adversely affected Indian farmers after the 1991 reforms
value: NCERT statement, no year, no number, no MSP data
source: NCERT keec103 ch.3, 'Agriculture' under Appraisal of reforms
note: Dated judgement about the reform period. Today's MSP numbers (claims M01-M08) cannot be read as supporting or refuting it without a time series; MSP series at CACP (cacp.da.gov.in/Home/MSP) is a JavaScript table not read here.

claim: NCERT chapters read contain no definition of CACP, FAQ, cost concepts A2/A2+FL/C2, the list of 22 crops, open-ended procurement, Price Support Scheme or PM-AASHA, and no mention of the Swaminathan Commission or the Shanta Kumar committee
value: Zero text hits for each term across 12 NCERT chapter files (keec102,103,105; jess104,201,202,204,205; legy203; lesy204; hess403)
note: 'support price' occurs in exactly four files (keec105, jess104, jess201, keec103). Class IX Economics ch.4 Food Security (known to cover MSP and buffer stock) could not be fetched: codes iess1-iess4 return 404. See open items.

claim: The Agricultural Prices Commission was set up by a Ministry of Food and Agriculture resolution dated 8 January 1965, renamed Commission for Agricultural Costs & Prices (CACP) by a resolution of 18 March 1985, and its terms of reference were revised by resolutions of 5 March 1980 and 30 July 2009
value: Set up by executive resolution, 8 Jan 1965 (No.6-2/65-C(E)); renamed 18 Mar 1985; ToR revised 5 Mar 1980 and 30 Jul 2009; an attached office of the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
second_source: PIB 22 Jan 2015 (HLC executive summary: Agricultural Prices Commission created in 1965)
note: The Commission rests on a Ministry resolution, not an Act of Parliament, per its own page.

claim: CACP's mandate: recommend MSP for 22 agricultural commodities and the Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) of sugarcane; it submits five price policy reports (kharif, rabi, copra, raw jute, sugarcane)
value: 22 MSP crops: 7 cereals (paddy, wheat, maize, jowar, bajra, barley, ragi), 5 pulses (gram, tur/arhar, moong, urad, lentil/masur), 7 oilseeds (groundnut, rapeseed-mustard, soyabean, sesamum, sunflower, safflower, nigerseed), 3 commercial crops (cotton, copra, jute); plus sugarcane FRP
second_source: PIB 3 Feb 2026 (Lok Sabha reply): 14 kharif + 6 rabi + jute and copra = 22
note: CACP counts 7+5+7+3 = 22; PIB counts 14+6+2 = 22. Same 22. NCERT names none of them.

claim: Each year the Government fixes MSPs for 22 mandated crops on CACP's recommendation, after considering the views of State Governments and central ministries
value: 22 crops; CACP recommends; Government (CCEA) decides
as_of: 3 Feb 2026 (Lok Sabha reply by MoS Agriculture)
source: PIB, Lok Sabha written reply, Ramnath Thakur, 3 Feb 2026
second_source: Lok Sabha Unstarred Q.1598, 28 Jul 2026, answer (a)&(b)

claim: Each season's MSP is approved by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), chaired by the Prime Minister
value: Kharif 2026-27 approved 13 May 2026; Rabi 2027-28 approved 30 Sep 2026
second_source: PIB, Rabi MSP release

claim: None of the official sources read cites an Act of Parliament as the basis of the MSP; the Government's replies describe MSP as a policy fixed by the Government each year, and no reply read announces a statutory guarantee
value: Lok Sabha Q.1598 part (c) asks whether the Government proposes a legal framework or statutory guarantee for MSP; the answer to (c) lists existing measures and does not say it will legislate
source: Lok Sabha Unstarred Q.1598 (28 Jul 2026), answer (c); Rajya Sabha reply 3 Feb 2023 'Legal Guarantee for MSP'
second_source: PIB 3 Feb 2023 (Rajya Sabha written reply)
note: A negative ('no Act exists') cannot be confirmed from replies alone. Needs a legal reviewer or a search of the Legislative Department / India Code. Teach as 'MSP is announced by the Government on CACP advice; it is a policy, not a right written in an Act' only after R1 review.

claim: Sugarcane has a Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP), not an MSP, and the FRP is determined under the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966
value: FRP 2026-27 = Rs 365 per quintal at 10.25% basic recovery rate; premium Rs 3.56/qtl per 0.1% above 10.25%; no deduction below 9.5% recovery (farmers get Rs 338.3/qtl); applies to cane bought from 1 Oct 2026
second_source: PIB 24 Jul 2019: 'The FRP of sugarcane is determined under Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966'
note: The Order's own text was not opened (India Code unreachable). The 1966 Order is cited by PIB only. Sugarcane FRP price payable by mills is the one farm price in this topic with a stated legal basis; teach the contrast only after the Order is read.

claim: FRP 2026-27: the A2+FL cost of sugarcane is Rs 182/qtl and the FRP of Rs 365/qtl is 100.5% above it
value: A2+FL Rs 182/qtl; FRP Rs 365/qtl; margin 100.5%
note: One source. PIB itself names the cost concept A2+FL here.

claim: MSP for toria and for de-husked coconut is not separately recommended; it is fixed from the MSP of rapeseed-mustard and of copra respectively
value: Toria from rapeseed & mustard; de-husked coconut from copra
source: PIB backgrounder 10 Oct 2025; PIB Rajya Sabha reply 7 Feb 2020
second_source: PIB 7 Feb 2020

claim: Perishable farm produce such as vegetables and fruits has no MSP; it is covered by the Market Intervention Scheme (MIS) on a State's request, triggered when ruling market prices fall at least 10% below the previous normal year
value: MIS for perishables not under MSP; at least 10% fall in ruling price; since 2024-25 a Price Differential Payment option and a storage-and-transport reimbursement for tomato, onion, potato
second_source: Lok Sabha Q.244, 22 Jul 2025 answer (f)-(g); PIB 18 Sep 2024

claim: The three 2020 farm laws were repealed by the Farm Laws Repeal Act 2021: the Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement on Price Assurance and Farm Services Act 2020, the Farmers' Produce Trade and Commerce (Promotion and Facilitation) Act 2020 and the Essential Commodities (Amendment) Act 2020
value: Repeal Bill introduced and passed in the Winter Session 2021; Section 3 also omits sub-section (1A) of section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act 1955
source: Farm Laws Repeal Bill 2021 (Bill No.143 of 2021) as introduced in Lok Sabha; PIB Winter Session summary
second_source: PIB, Winter Session 2021 adjourned sine die
note: Bill text read at a PRS copy of the Lok Sabha document. The Act's enactment date and number at India Code could not be read (UNVERIFIED, see O06). The Statement of Objects says the Government's policy 'for the first time' fixed MSP at least 1.5 times cost; quote as Government's statement.

claim: On 19 Nov 2021 the Prime Minister announced the repeal of the three laws and a committee to promote zero-budget (natural) farming, change crop pattern as the country's needs change, and make MSP more effective and transparent, with representatives of the Centre, States, farmers, agricultural scientists and economists
value: Announcement 19 Nov 2021
source: PIB, PM's address to the Nation 19 Nov 2021
second_source: PIB 26 Jul 2022 (Lok Sabha reply: 'The Government has formed a Committee ...')

claim: The Committee on MSP and related topics (reported as chaired by former Agriculture Secretary Sanjay Agrawal, constituted 18 Jul 2022) has not published a report as of July 2026
value: No official document read giving constitution date, chair, members, terms of reference or status
source: Only news reports (Newslaundry 8 Jul 2026 and others, not evidence) and PIB 26 Jul 2022 confirm that a committee was formed
note: Rajya Sabha reply of 7 Feb 2025 (PQ 267) could not be read (rsdebate.nic.in returned a web-app shell, not the PDF). Needs the Ministry notification or a Rajya Sabha/Lok Sabha reply; ask lead to open sansad.in in a browser. Do not name members or chair on screen until read at source.

claim: The Lok Sabha reply of 28 Jul 2026 to a question asking whether the Government will enact a legal framework with a statutory MSP guarantee describes existing measures (MSP for 22 crops, 50% minimum margin, procurement, PM-AASHA, MIS) and notes that agriculture is a State subject; it does not announce legislation
value: Question by Shri Rajabhau Parag Prakash Waje; answer by MoS Shri Ramnath Thakur
second_source: PIB 3 Feb 2023 Rajya Sabha reply (same pattern: describes mechanism)
note: Describe only what the reply says. Do not paraphrase as 'the Government refuses' or 'the Government agrees'.

claim: MoSPI's NSS 77th round report defines MSP as a form of market intervention by the Government of India to insure agricultural producers against any sharp fall in farm prices, announced at the beginning of the sowing season for certain crops on CACP's recommendation
value: Definition in the survey's concepts section
note: One source; a statistical agency's working definition. Good plain-words anchor for the 'floor under the price' idea. 'At the beginning of the sowing season' fits the announcement dates read (13 May and 30 Sep 2026).

claim: Union Budget 2018-19 announced that MSP for all unannounced kharif crops would be kept at least one and a half times their production cost, as a pre-determined principle; the speech also said NITI Aayog with Centre and States would put in place a mechanism so farmers get adequate price when market price is below MSP
value: Budget speech 1 Feb 2018, paras 13-14
source: Union Budget 2018-19, Speech of the Finance Minister, paras 13-14
second_source: PIB Lok Sabha reply 3 Feb 2026; Lok Sabha Q.244 answer (a)
note: The speech does not define 'production cost'. Para 13 also refers to a party manifesto: leave that out (guardrail: no party attribution).

claim: From 2018-19 the Government set MSPs of all mandated kharif, rabi and commercial crops to give a minimum return of 50% over the all-India weighted average cost of production
value: At least 50% over all-India weighted average cost of production
second_source: Lok Sabha Q.244 (22 Jul 2025) answer (a); Lok Sabha Q.1598 (28 Jul 2026)
note: The margin is on the all-India weighted average, not per State or per farmer.

claim: The cost on which the 50% return is reckoned is A2+FL; CACP also computes C2 but uses it only as a benchmark to see whether recommended MSPs cover it in some major producing States
value: 'CACP considers both A2+FL and C2 costs while recommending MSPs. CACP reckons only A2+FL cost for return. However, C2 costs are used by CACP primarily as benchmark reference costs'
source: PIB 7 Feb 2020, Agriculture Minister's reply 'Formula for fixing MSP for Paddy and Wheat'
second_source: CACP KMS 2026-27 Table S.1 headings: 'Projected A2+FL Cost' and 'MSP as percent of A2+FL'; PIB footnote to each MSP release (cost includes paid-out costs and imputed value of family labour)
note: Key claim: two sources agree. The 2020 text is six years old; the 2026 releases and CACP tables still apply A2+FL, so the position is unchanged.

claim: CACP's definitions: A2 is paid-out cost; A2+FL adds the imputed value of family labour; C2 adds to A2+FL the rental value of owned land (net of land revenue) and interest on fixed capital excluding land
value: A2 = paid-out cost; A2+FL = A2 + imputed family labour; C2 = A2+FL + rental value of owned land (net of land revenue) + interest on fixed capital excluding land
source: CACP, Price Policy for Kharif Crops KMS 2025-26, list of acronyms
second_source: CACP 'Cost Concepts' note: Cost A2 = A1 + rent paid for leased-in land; B1 = A1 + interest on owned fixed capital (excl. land); B2 = B1 + rental value of owned land (net of land revenue) + rent for leased land; C2 = B2 + imputed value of family labour; C2* and C3 also defined
note: Both CACP sources agree. The Cost Concepts note labels more items (A1, B1, B2, C1, C2*, C3). Teach A2, A2+FL, C2 only; the SYLLABUS and press use these three.

claim: Family labour is imputed at the statutory wage rate or the actual market rate, whichever is higher
value: Imputation rule for family labour
source: CACP, Cost Concepts, section 2 Imputation Methods table
note: One source. Page image read (text layer is unreadable).

claim: The Government's replies say the cost formula is uniform for all 22 mandated crops and all States, MSP is one all-India price, and cost is taken as an all-India weighted average
value: Uniform formula; not region specific; all-India weighted average
second_source: PIB 10 Oct 2025 backgrounder: 'cost formula ... uniform for all 22 mandated crops and states'
note: CACP's State-wise costs (claim F10) differ widely, so one national MSP leaves different margins in different States.

claim: CACP weighs these factors when recommending MSP: cost of production, demand and supply, domestic and world prices, inter-crop price parity, terms of trade between agriculture and non-agriculture, effect on the rest of the economy including cost of living, rational use of land and water, and a minimum 50% margin over cost of production
value: Factors as listed by CACP
second_source: PIB 7 Feb 2020; PIB 10 Oct 2025

claim: Paddy KMS 2026-27 costs per quintal: A2 Rs 1,288; A2+FL Rs 1,627; C2 Rs 2,162; the common-paddy MSP of Rs 2,441 is 150% of A2+FL and, by our own division, about 113% of C2
value: A2 1288; A2+FL 1627; C2 2162; MSP 2441; MSP/A2+FL = 1.500; MSP/C2 = 1.129 (calculated by us)
source: CACP, Price Policy for Kharif Crops KMS 2026-27, Table 5.4 and Table S.1
page_or_section: Table 5.4 (printed p.141, PDF p.167); Table S.1 (PDF p.23)
second_source: PIB 13 May 2026: cost Rs 1,627, MSP Rs 2,441, margin 50%
note: Image of Table 5.4 read by eye. The C2 comparison is our arithmetic (2441/2162) and is not printed by CACP: label as 'worked out from two published numbers'.

claim: Wheat RMS 2027-28 (crop year 2026-27) costs per quintal: A2+FL Rs 1,264; C2 Rs 1,849; PIB prints a 106% margin; CACP Table S.1 prints 207% of A2+FL; our division of the rounded figures (2610/1264) gives 206.5%; by our division the MSP is about 141% of C2

page_or_section: Table 5.6 (printed p.114-115, PDF p.138-139); Table S.1 (PDF p.21)
second_source: PIB 30 Sep 2026: cost Rs 1,264, MSP Rs 2,610, margin 106%
note: A2+FL and C2 for wheat verified by image (text para 5.26). A2 1011 read by OCR only. Audit fix 2 Nov 2026.

claim: State-wise projected A2+FL cost of paddy for KMS 2026-27 ranges from Rs 1,030/qtl (Punjab, lowest) to Rs 3,707/qtl (Maharashtra, highest); nine of the 18 States costed, accounting for 42% of production, have A2+FL cost below the all-India average
value: Range 1030 to 3707 per quintal; 9 of 18 States; 42% of production
note: Image read. Quote numbers, not a ranking of States: the CACP gives yield and cost of cultivation as the reason. No mocking any State.

claim: The National Commission on Farmers (chair M.S. Swaminathan) recommended that MSP should be at least 50% more than the weighted average cost of production; the Ministry told Rajya Sabha in 2020 that the National Policy for Farmers 2007, when finalised, did not include this 50% recommendation
value: NCF recommendation as stated by the Ministry; cost concept not named in the Ministry's sentence
source: PIB 7 Feb 2020, Agriculture Minister's written reply in Rajya Sabha
second_source: PRS India summary of the NCF Fifth Report (think-tank summary, NOT evidence on its own): MSP should be at least 50% more than the weighted average cost of production
note: The NCF Fifth and Final Report (4 Oct 2006) itself was NOT read at a government host; the PARI copy is not accepted. So what the NCF means by 'cost' (C2 or not) is UNVERIFIED, see F12. The 2007 policy sentence is the Ministry's wording about an earlier Government: quote it without naming parties.

claim: What cost concept the National Commission on Farmers meant (the widely repeated 'C2 plus 50%') is not stated in any official text read in this run
value: UNVERIFIED: no primary text read for NCF's cost concept
source: National Commission on Farmers, Fifth and Final Report, Oct 2006 (not obtained)
note: Searched agriwelfare.gov.in and agricoop paths; no document served. Needs the report from the Ministry's archive or a library copy. Until then say only: 'the Commission recommended at least 50% above the weighted average cost of production; the Government's stated policy applies 50% to A2+FL'.

claim: Common paddy MSP for Kharif Marketing Season (KMS) 2026-27 is Rs 2,441 per quintal (Grade A Rs 2,461), up Rs 72 from Rs 2,369 in 2025-26 and from Rs 1,310 in 2013-14
value: Common Rs 2,441; Grade A Rs 2,461; +Rs 72 over 2025-26; Rs 1,310 in 2013-14 (+86%); A2+FL cost Rs 1,627; margin 50%
second_source: CACP Price Policy KMS 2026-27, Table S.1
note: All 14 crops cross-checked PIB vs CACP (28 cells, all equal). Full table in docs/upsc/living/AGR-07.csv.

value: Rs 2,585; A2+FL cost Rs 1,239; margin 109%; previous Rs 2,425
second_source: PIB backgrounder 10 Oct 2025 table

value: As listed

claim: Largest rises in kharif MSP for 2026-27: sunflower seed +Rs 622, cotton (medium) +Rs 557, nigerseed +Rs 515, sesamum +Rs 500; the smallest: moong +Rs 12 (0.1%) and maize +Rs 10 (0.4%)
value: As listed
second_source: CACP Table S.1: moong +0.1%, maize +0.4%

claim: Paddy MSP rose from Rs 1,940 (KMS 2021-22) to Rs 2,369 (KMS 2025-26) while CACP's A2+FL cost rose from Rs 1,293 to Rs 1,579; wheat MSP rose from Rs 1,975 to Rs 2,425 while cost rose from Rs 960 to Rs 1,182

claim: Paddy and wheat are bought by the Food Corporation of India and State agencies; pulses, oilseeds and copra by NAFED and NCCF (under the Price Support Scheme); cotton by the Cotton Corporation of India; jute by the Jute Corporation of India; coarse grains for the Central Pool by State agencies
value: Agencies as listed

second_source: PIB 10 Oct 2025 'Procurement Mechanisms'

claim: Rice is procured under two systems: Centralised (non-DCP: FCI directly or through State agencies) and Decentralised Procurement (DCP: the State procures, stores and distributes under the National Food Security Act and other welfare schemes, handing excess to FCI); the Centre reimburses States on laid-down norms

second_source: CACP KMS 2026-27 para 2.32-2.33

claim: How many States are under DCP: the March 2026 Kharif report says 16 States for rice are under DCP and 7 States/UTs non-DCP; the July 2026 Rabi report says 18 States/UTs for rice and 9 States for wheat are under DCP
value: Rice DCP: 16 States (CACP KMS 2026-27, Mar 2026) against 18 States/UTs (CACP RMS 2027-28, Jul 2026)
source: CACP KMS 2026-27 para 2.32 and RMS 2027-28 para 2.28
second_source: CACP KMS 2026-27
note: Two CACP reports four months apart give different counts and cite Annex tables (2.1 and 2.3) that were not read. Use the later (18 rice, 9 wheat) only after reading the annex.

value: PSS trigger: price below MSP; ceiling 25% of national production; tur, urad, masur up to 100% of the State's production
second_source: PIB 17 Feb 2025; PIB 10 Oct 2025
note: Cotton and jute have no maximum limit (PIB 10 Oct 2025). Audit fix 2 Nov 2026.

value: 100% procurement of the State's tur, urad and masur through NAFED and NCCF for the next four years
source: PIB, Cabinet decision 1 Oct 2025; PIB 17 Feb 2025
second_source: PIB 17 Feb 2025; PIB 10 Oct 2025
note: 'Four years' from 2025-26 ends 2028-29, as PIB 10 Oct 2025 says.

claim: PM-AASHA was approved by the Cabinet on 12 Sep 2018, announced in Budget 2018 to make MSP effective; components then: Price Support Scheme, Price Deficiency Payment Scheme, pilot Private Procurement and Stockist Scheme; the Cabinet raised the Government guarantee by Rs 16,550 crore to Rs 45,550 crore
value: Origin 12 Sep 2018
second_source: PIB 18 Sep 2024 (continuation, components now PSS, PSF, PDPS, MIS)
